strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: improving short quaternary insertion/deletion/substitution codes, where asymptotically efficient constructions can have substantial redundancy. Using learned embeddings to guide explicit codebook construction is a useful research direction.

Algorithm 1 removes neighbors using exact Levenshtein distance, ensuring minimum distance at least three independently of embedding accuracy. This provides a sound foundation for the constructed codes.

Table 1 demonstrates consistent improvements over random selection across ten runs, with average cardinality gains of 6.4–15.8%. The best length-11 code contains 36,368 codewords and achieves a rate of approximately 68.9%. The original-versus-revised loss comparison provides a relevant ablation.

Table 2 provides substantial empirical evidence for decoding reliability, reporting zero failures in 10^8 single-edit trials when querying four neighbors. The algorithms and tables make the pipeline understandable, and the source-code link and synthetic data generation support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central justification for the selection score is technically incorrect. Batch normalization does not imply a multivariate Gaussian embedding distribution. Even under Gaussianity, density under the original candidate distribution need not track the number of conflicting neighbors remaining during greedy selection. Greedy selection produces a maximal codebook, without guaranteeing maximum cardinality. The binary t-SNE visualization does not establish these properties; direct correlations between the score and exact neighborhood counts are needed.

The construction baselines do not adequately establish the contribution of learning. Comparisons against exact neighborhood-count heuristics, minimum-degree selection, and local search would be more informative than random selection alone. Figure 4 also does not explain how the asymptotic redundancy expressions for prior constructions are instantiated at these very short lengths. The novelty discussion should better distinguish the method from classical greedy code construction, existing neural edit embeddings, and codebook generation work such as [17].

The optimality claims exceed the evidence. Agreement with log2(n) + log2(log2(n)) + log2(3) over a few short lengths does not establish minimal redundancy. The substitution sphere-packing bound gives |C| <= 4^n/(1+3n), which at n=11 is approximately 123,362, versus 36,368 achieved. This bound leaves considerable uncertainty about optimality, and no tighter IDS-specific bound or exact small-instance optimum is supplied. Acknowledging the absence of a proof is appropriate, but the repeated optimality conclusions still require qualification.

The decoding comparison omits simple exact alternatives. For a single-edit channel, one can enumerate O(n) possible inverse edits of the received sequence and check membership in a codebook hash table, avoiding a scan over every codeword. Likewise, checking whether edit distance is at most one takes linear time; hardness results for unrestricted edit distance do not establish difficulty in this regime. Consequently, speedups over the chosen brute-force baseline do not establish a compelling advantage for neural decoding.

The advertised combination of reliable correction and O(n) decoding is not established. Logarithmic expected k-d-tree query time requires assumptions that are not verified for the 64-dimensional embeddings. Figure 5 reports an increase from 6 to 367 seconds as n increases from 7 to 11, providing no convincing evidence of linear scaling. The k=1 configuration fails on approximately 0.3–0.9% of trials, while the paper assigns O(n^2) verification cost to the multiple-neighbor configuration. Exhaustive verification of the few million possible single-edit cases would strengthen the reliability claim.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete in the manuscript despite the code link. Missing information includes the full network configuration, training schedule, training-pair distribution and sample counts, handling of lengths n-1 and n+1, and edit-type sampling probabilities. Hardware, timing boundaries, construction time, and peak memory are also needed to assess the efficiency claims.

The experiments establish results for isolated, short, single-edit segments. They do not evaluate segment-boundary recovery or outer-code overhead, so the implications for overall segmented-channel performance and storage density remain unverified. This limits the demonstrated practical significance beyond the useful inner-code construction results.
